activities.anchor: the meaning of a whole is built from the senses of its parts
activities.caption: pair each Fregean term with its work
activities.name: langFregeMatch

config.prompt: Sense, reference and their consequences — pair them:

pairs.right: the thing picked out — both Venus names terminate here
the mode of presentation — how the thing is given
sense, arguably, with no existing bearer
whole sentences built from the senses of their parts — formal semantics' founding principle

config.why: The distinction explains why some identity statements are discoveries — and only sense explains informativeness.

activities.anchor: Two different readings, once invisible, are separated by the scope of the negation
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the Russell gloss
activities.name: langRussellSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's gloss on Russell is wrong — click it:
lines: Russell's target: 'The present king of France is bald' — a phrase that names nothing.
The sentence is meaningless, because its subject does not exist.
Russell's rewrite: 'there exists exactly one present king of France, and whatever is such a king is bald.'
The sentence is simply false — its first conjunct fails.
Method lesson: surface grammar systematically misleads about logical form.
config.correction: Under the analysis the sentence is false, not meaningless — and its negation ('the present king of France is not bald') comes out true.
config.why: Philosophy's job is to expose the bones beneath the surface — analysis as method.

activities.anchor: Philosophy, on this view, is therapy
activities.caption: file each claim — early or late Wittgenstein
activities.name: langWittSort

config.prompt: Picture, then use — file each claim under its Wittgenstein:

items.label: a meaningful proposition pictures a possible state of affairs
language mirrors the logical structure of the world
ethics, aesthetics and the mystical lie outside the world of facts
meaning is use within a language game — a social practice with rules and purposes
'game' has no single essence, only overlapping family resemblance
the private language argument: no public standard of correctness, no meaning

config.why: One philosopher dismantled his earlier self — and the use view comes with teeth: without a public standard of correctness there is no meaning at all.

activities.anchor: just as a promise fails if made to a doorknob
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the anatomy of a speech act
activities.name: langSpeechCloze

config.text: Every utterance has a %%0%% content (what is said), an %%1%% force (what is done in saying it — asserting, warning, promising, ordering), and a %%2%% effect (what it causes). And speech acts come with felicity conditions: the ship-naming fails if the speaker lacks %%3%%.
config.hint: Said, done-in-saying, caused — and what the ship-namer needed.

activities.anchor: the most destabilising paper of the century
activities.caption: true or false — chains, webs and maxims
activities.name: langKripkeJudge

statements.s: Names abbreviate descriptions in the speaker's head.
statements.why: Kripke's causal-historical chains replace descriptivism — a name refers even if every description you associate with it is false.

statements.s: 'Water is H2O' is a necessary a posteriori truth — discovered by chemistry, yet true in every possible world with water.
statements.why: Necessity and knowability come apart — Kripke's new category.

statements.s: For Quine, no sentence is immune to revision — our statements face experience as a corporate web.
statements.why: 'Two Dogmas' made meaning holistic and forced everyone to say what they meant by 'meaning'.

statements.s: 'Can you pass the salt?' is a grammar query.
statements.why: Implicature: conversation runs on cooperative maxims whose violations are themselves informative.

activities.anchor: religious language is its own language game
activities.caption: walk the century's readings of one sentence
activities.name: langGodBranch

config.root: One sentence — 'God exists'. Walk the readings the machinery produces.

start.text: The verificationist verdict on the sentence?

choices.label: Neither true nor false — meaningless, like an expression of emotion
False — the evidence is against it

falsey.text: Ayer's claim was stronger still: not false, but outside truth-apt discourse entirely.

ayer.text: And the verification principle on its own test?

choices.label: It fails — itself neither analytic nor empirically verifiable
It passes — meaning needs only clarity

passes.text: Elegant and notoriously self-undermining — the principle fails its own test.

flew.text: Flew's challenge: a claim admitting no imaginable count-evidence 'dies the death of a thousand qualifications.' Which reply makes it checkable?

choices.label: Hick's eschatological verification — checkable at the end of an afterlife
Hare's bliks — fundamental stances, not claims

blik.text: Bliks are not the kind of thing verification touches — a corrupted blik is not a wrong belief about evidence.

mitchell.text: Mitchell's partisan: faith as trust that acknowledges contrary evidence but holds anyway — the middle position.

config.why: Machinery, not eloquence, decides — and the Wittgensteinian wing dissolves the frame entirely, judging the sentence by its own criteria of use.

activities.anchor: which is why philosophy of language is the load-bearing course for philosophy of religion
activities.caption: pair each reading with its verdict on 'God is love'
activities.name: langFiveMatch

config.prompt: One sentence, five readings — pair each school with its verdict:

pairs.right: a proposition — true or false depending on God's nature
neither analytic nor empirically verifiable — meaningless
verifiable, if true, at the end of things
a stance colouring every interpretation — not a claim at all
its own language game — intelligibility settled by its role in the practice

config.why: The speech-act reading finds illocutionary force (a vow, an avowal); the Fregean question undercuts them all — what, if anything, does 'God' refer to?
